Students who survived the screening and subsequent examinations were in line for a $1,500 stipend to finance graduate work in humanities and social science [Source 1].

answer.text:
In January 1980, the Stuyvesant Hall Governing Board unanimously adopted a security policy requiring that only Stuyvesant Hall residents be admitted to the building after 11:30 p.m. [Source 1]. Any non-resident entering the building after that time had to be escorted by a Stuyvesant resident [Source 1]. Unescorted visitors were required to call the resident they were visiting, who then had to come to the lobby and escort them inside [Source 1]. Student security aides were stationed on duty until 7 a.m. to check student identification cards against a master list of residents, using dorm-coded keys to confirm residency if a student did not have an ID card [Source 1].

Stuyvesant Hall resident life counselor Bill Herndon (also identified as Lewis Herndon) stated that the internal procedure was established to identify individuals responsible for violence and vandalism, which occurred after late-night non-resident visitors wandered into the dorm [Source 1, Source 2]. Following the implementation of the escort policy, Herndon noted that individual billings for dorm damages increased relative to hall-wide billings [Source 2].

answer.text: At the 1982 All-Ohio meet at Ohio State, the Ohio Wesleyan women's track team set three new school relay records [Source 1]. The 880-yard relay team—comprising sophomore Pebbles Muller, freshmen Amanda Osborn and Lynn Rhoden, and senior Sabrina Spencer—placed sixth while bettering the 1979 OWU record of 1:51.2 by one second [Source 1]. The distance medley relay team—made up of freshmen Liz Einfeldt, Nena Lenfest, and Barb Sweeney, along with junior Margie Morris—placed fifth with a time of 13:17.1, breaking the previous year's mark of 13:18 [Source 1]. answer.text:
## Addressing Outdated Communications Infrastructure in 1987

By 1987, Ohio Wesleyan University faced significant operational challenges due to its phone system, which had been installed in 1974 and relied on a central campus switchboard rather than direct dialing [1987-03-25-25]. Students, faculty, and local businesses reported frequent delays, missing dial tones, lost calls, and persistently busy lines when attempting to reach campus offices or dormitory rooms [1987-03-25-25, 1987-10-14-3]. Physical Plant Director John Tombarge initially estimated that replacing the entire setup would cost approximately $1.2 million [1987-03-25-25].

To address these infrastructure shortcomings, the OWU Board of Trustees authorized $50,000 in late September 1987 for a formal feasibility study [1987-09-30-0]. ![Trustees begin to gather Saturday morning for their meeting.](https://pub-6b4b0bceb63e48c1af6578ad09beb2e5.r2.dev/1987-09-30/images/0001_Page%201_img1.webp) Vice President of Business Affairs Louis Szalontai stated that this allocation covered hiring a professional telecommunications consultant to research modern system technologies and evaluate the costs of leasing or purchasing a new system [1987-10-14-3]. The university targeted completing the complete telecommunications overhaul by 1992 as part of its broader Five-Year Plan [1987-10-14-3].

## Consolidating Academic Support Services in 2000

In the fall of 2000, Ohio Wesleyan addressed its previously fragmented academic support structure by establishing the central Academic Resource Center (ARC) on the third floor of the R.W. Corns Building [2000-09-13-3]. The initiative brought together three separate or inactive campus learning entities under a single unified roof: the Writing Resource Center and the Academic Skills Office, both previously housed separately in University Hall, and the Qualitative Skills Center, which had formerly operated out of Ham-Wil before being inactive for several years [2000-09-13-3].

Led by Director Donna Dawson, the centralized center equipped students with a shared reference library, computer stations, and dedicated study space [2000-09-13-3]. The ARC provided coordinated support across multiple disciplines, offering guidance on writing and standardized testing, instruction in organizational skills and stress management, and math and economics tutoring [2000-09-13-3].

answer.text:
Austin Hall originally closed in 1984. In the fall of 1986, plans were established to renovate the former residence hall into Austin Manor, a living unit intended for both students and retired alumni [Source 1]. Financing for the restoration was put together in 1987, but work could not begin without tax credit approval based on the building's historic site status [Source 1].

While the Interior Department enthusiastically approved declaring Austin Hall a historic site in the state of Ohio, the Philadelphia office initially turned down the tax credit [Source 1]. Upon appeal, the tax credit was successfully approved, allowing restoration work to commence [Source 1]. At the January 1988 faculty meeting, University President David Warren estimated that the restored building would be ready for an occupant by November or December [Source 1].

answer.text:
## Learning Focus and Audience

In 1997, the Early Childhood Center (ECC), located at Park Avenue and Franklin Street, provided hands-on learning support for preschool children aged three to five while offering practical work experience to Ohio Wesleyan University students [1997-01-22-17]. ![an OWU student assists a child with a project at the Early Childhood Center](https://pub-6b4b0bceb63e48c1af6578ad09beb2e5.r2.dev/1997-01-22/images/0005_Page%205_img1.webp) Directed by Dr. Leslie Mass, the center served 110 families and employed 29 OWU students through work-study and Student Assistantship programs to support the children's growth [1997-01-22-17]. In contrast, the Academic Resource Center (ARC), established in fall 2000 on the third floor of the R. W. Corns Building, was created to provide direct academic support to OWU undergraduate students [2000-09-13-3]. Directed by Donna Dawson, the ARC focused on collegiate academic success rather than early childhood development [2000-09-13-3].

## Instructional Approach and Environment

The ECC emphasized sensory exploration, imaginative play, and flexible, child-led learning rather than a formal, rigid curriculum [1997-01-22-17]. Children participated in hands-on activities such as constructing miniature houses, cutting apples for snacks, observing and feeding mice or worms in three classroom aquariums, and developing projects around their interests, such as leaf studies following nature walks [1997-01-22-17]. The ECC also encouraged peer support, empowering older children to help younger ones when they faced challenges [1997-01-22-17]. Conversely, the ARC offered structured, task-oriented academic support designed for university coursework [2000-09-13-3]. Its facility housed study space, three computers, and a reference library where students could receive targeted instruction and assistance [2000-09-13-3].

## Service Structure and Organizational Scope

While the ECC operated as an interactive preschool environment that utilized campus field trips to university science labs, art studios, and athletic facilities, the ARC functioned as a centralized academic hub consolidating three previously separate campus resources [1997-01-22-17, 2000-09-13-3]. The ARC combined the Writing Resource Center, which offered assistance on papers, resumes, and test preparation; the Academic Skills Office, which provided help with organizational skills, test preparation, and stress management; and the revived Qualitative Skills Center, which delivered tutoring for math courses up to Calculus II as well as economics [2000-09-13-3]. Additionally, the ARC planned future expansion to accommodate students with learning disabilities, illustrating a centralized, multi-branch support model for college academics in contrast to the ECC's experiential, community-oriented preschool model [2000-09-13-3].
